questions.stem: When psychologists distinguish sex from gender, 'sex' refers to:
options: the behaviours that a culture expects of males and females
a person's inner sense of being male, female or another gender
beliefs about what males and females are typically like
biological features such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy
questions.explanation: Sex refers to biological characteristics: sex chromosomes, hormones and reproductive anatomy. Expected behaviours are gender roles, and a person's inner sense is gender identity.

questions.stem: Gender identity is best defined as:
options: a person's own sense of their gender
the set of behaviours society expects
the sex chromosomes a person inherits
a fixed belief about one sex as a group
questions.explanation: Gender identity is a person's internal sense of their own gender. It is distinct from biological sex and from gender roles, which are the behaviours a society expects.

questions.stem: A belief that 'boys are naturally better at maths than girls' is an example of:
options: an intersex condition
androgyny
a gender stereotype
a gender identity
questions.explanation: A gender stereotype is a generalised, often oversimplified belief about the characteristics of males or females as groups. It is applied to individuals regardless of their actual abilities.

questions.stem: In a community, women are expected to do most of the cooking and caring while men are expected to earn the income. These expectations are:
options: sex differences
intersex conditions
gender roles
gender identities
questions.explanation: Gender roles are the behaviours, tasks and responsibilities a society considers appropriate for males and females. They vary between cultures and change over time.

questions.stem: According to Bem, a person who scores high on both masculine traits (such as assertiveness) and feminine traits (such as nurturance) is:
options: sex-typed
cross-sex-typed
androgynous
undifferentiated
questions.explanation: Bem described androgyny as having high levels of both masculine and feminine characteristics. A person low on both is undifferentiated, and a person high on only the traits expected of their sex is sex-typed.

questions.stem: An intersex condition is one in which a person:
options: shows high levels of both masculine and feminine personality traits
has been raised in a family with no clear gender roles at all
has sex characteristics that do not fit typical male or female
identifies with a gender different from the one assigned at birth
questions.explanation: Intersex conditions involve variations in sex chromosomes, hormones or anatomy that do not fit typical binary definitions of male or female. They are biological variations, not gender identities or personality patterns.

questions.stem: Klinefelter syndrome occurs in people who have which sex chromosomes?
options: XXY
XO
XYY
XX
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome occurs in males with an extra X chromosome (XXY). XO is Turner syndrome, which affects females.

questions.stem: Which characteristics are typical of Klinefelter syndrome?
options: female appearance with internal testes and no menstruation at puberty
female appearance at birth followed by male development at puberty
male appearance with no differences in hormones or fertility at all
male appearance with lower testosterone, small testes and usually infertility
questions.explanation: People with Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) are male in appearance but tend to have lower testosterone, small testes and infertility, and may develop some breast tissue. Most identify as male.

questions.stem: In the Batista family in the Dominican Republic, studied by Imperato-McGinley and colleagues (1974), some XY children appeared female at birth because of:
options: high levels of androgens produced by their adrenal glands in the womb
cells that could not respond to any androgens throughout life
an enzyme deficiency that stopped testosterone becoming DHT
an extra X chromosome inherited from their mother before birth
questions.explanation: The children had 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, so testosterone was not converted into DHT, which shapes external male genitals before birth. A surge of testosterone at puberty then caused male development.

questions.stem: Most of the Batista children who had been raised as girls adopted a male gender identity after puberty. What does this suggest?
options: Gender identity is fixed only by the way children are raised early on
Gender roles are the same in every culture across the whole world
Chromosomes have no role at all in the development of gender
Biological factors such as hormones influence gender identity
questions.explanation: Despite being raised as girls, most changed to a male identity when their bodies masculinised at puberty, which supports a strong biological influence. Critics note the community already recognised the condition, so social factors may also have played a part.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of using the Batista family as evidence for the biological argument?
options: The study used a large random sample, so results cannot be applied to individuals
The researchers controlled the children's hormone levels with a placebo condition
Their community knew the condition, so social expectations may have shaped the change
The children were too young to report their own gender identity in interviews
questions.explanation: The condition was recognised locally, so families and the community may have expected the children to become men, which is a social influence. It is also a small, unusual group, which limits generalisation.

questions.stem: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) in a genetic female (XX) involves:
options: cells that cannot respond to androgens such as testosterone
a missing X chromosome that prevents puberty from starting
exposure to unusually high levels of androgens before birth
an extra X chromosome that lowers testosterone production
questions.explanation: In CAH the adrenal glands produce excess androgens from before birth. XX individuals may be born with partly masculinised genitals, though they have ovaries and a uterus.

questions.stem: Money and Ehrhardt (1972) studied girls with CAH. What did they report?
options: The girls were more often described as tomboyish, preferring rough play
The girls all adopted a male gender identity once they reached puberty
The girls showed no differences in play or interests from other girls
The girls showed lower verbal ability than girls without the condition
questions.explanation: Money and Ehrhardt reported that girls with CAH were more often described as tomboyish, with more interest in active play and less in dolls, though most identified as girls. This was taken as evidence that prenatal androgens influence gender-typed behaviour.

questions.stem: A critic argues that parents' knowledge of their daughters' CAH may have affected Money and Ehrhardt's findings. What is the critic's point?
options: The sample was too large to allow any detailed study of each child
Parents may have treated or described the girls differently, a social influence
The girls were exposed to too few androgens for any effect to be measured
Chromosomes, not hormones, must be the only cause of gender differences
questions.explanation: If parents knew of the condition, their expectations could shape how they raised the girls and how they reported their behaviour. This means social factors cannot be ruled out as a cause.

questions.stem: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), a person with XY chromosomes:
options: develops a female body because cells cannot respond to androgens
develops a male body but cannot produce enough of the hormone
develops female genitals that become male at the start of puberty
has an extra X chromosome and so develops a female appearance
questions.explanation: In complete AIS the body produces testosterone but its cells cannot respond to it, so the external body develops as female. The person usually has internal testes and no uterus.

questions.stem: People with complete AIS are usually raised as girls and usually have a female gender identity, despite XY chromosomes. What does this suggest?
options: Androgens have no effect on the developing body
Gender identity is set entirely by the Y chromosome
Gender identity cannot be studied in intersex people
Chromosomes alone do not determine gender identity
questions.explanation: AIS shows that having a Y chromosome does not by itself produce a male identity. The lack of androgen effects on the body, and being raised as girls, are both consistent with a female identity.

questions.stem: AIS is often first discovered in adolescence. Why?
options: Menstruation does not begin, because there is no uterus
Male features suddenly appear when puberty begins
The person develops much later than their classmates
Testosterone levels fall sharply during the teenage years
questions.explanation: With no uterus, a person with complete AIS does not menstruate, and medical investigation of this often reveals the condition. External development at puberty is otherwise typically female.

questions.stem: Harasty and colleagues examined the brains of men and women after death. What did they report about language areas?
options: Language was controlled only by the right hemisphere in women
There were no differences between the brains of men and women
Language-related areas were proportionally larger in women
Language-related areas were proportionally larger in men
questions.explanation: Harasty reported that cortical areas involved in language, including Broca's and Wernicke's areas, were proportionally larger in women. This was linked to the small average female advantage on some verbal tasks.

questions.stem: Kimura (1987) argued that sex differences in some abilities reflect differences in brain organisation. Which pattern did she describe?
options: Females on average do better on all tasks, as language uses both hemispheres
Females on average do better on verbal fluency; males on mental rotation
Males on average do better on verbal fluency; females on targeting tasks
Females and males show no average differences on verbal or spatial tasks
questions.explanation: Kimura reported that women on average perform better on tasks such as verbal fluency and perceptual speed, and men on average on tasks such as mental rotation and targeting. These are average differences with large overlap between individuals.

questions.stem: A report states that men on average outscore women on a mental rotation task. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: Many individual women will outscore many individual men on the task
Every man will outscore every woman who completes the task
The difference must be caused entirely by the brain at birth
The difference shows that the task was culturally biased
questions.explanation: Average group differences come with large overlap, so they cannot predict any one person's score. They also do not show the cause, because experience and practice may contribute.

questions.stem: A girl watches her mother fix a bike, is praised by her father when she helps, and later tries to fix her own bike. Which theory best explains this?
options: social learning theory (Bandura)
gender schema theory (Bem)
social role theory (Eagly)
sociobiological (evolutionary) theory
questions.explanation: Social learning theory explains gender behaviour through observing models and being reinforced for imitating them. The girl observes a model and is praised, so she reproduces the behaviour.

questions.stem: Eagly's social role theory proposes that sex differences in behaviour arise mainly because:
options: men and women have occupied different roles in society
boys and girls develop gender constancy at different ages
children sort information using mental gender categories
natural selection favoured different traits in each sex
questions.explanation: Eagly argued that the division of labour between men and women created different social roles, and expectations attached to those roles produce gender differences. As roles change, gender differences are expected to change too.

questions.stem: In Kohlberg's cognitive developmental theory, what is the correct order of stages?
options: gender constancy, gender stability, gender identity
gender identity, gender constancy, gender stability
gender identity, gender stability, gender constancy
gender stability, gender identity, gender constancy
questions.explanation: Children first label themselves as a boy or girl (identity), then understand gender stays the same over time (stability), and finally that it stays the same across situations and appearances (constancy).

questions.stem: A five-year-old says that a boy who grows his hair long and wears a dress would become a girl. According to Kohlberg, this child has not yet reached:
options: gender schema
gender constancy
gender identity
gender stability
questions.explanation: Gender constancy is the understanding that gender stays the same despite changes in appearance or activity. This child thinks appearance changes gender, so constancy has not been reached.

questions.stem: Kohlberg proposed that once children reach gender constancy they:
options: are no longer influenced by their own culture
actively seek out and copy same-gender models
stop paying any attention to gender in others
lose the gender identity they had before then
questions.explanation: Kohlberg argued that children socialise themselves once they understand their gender is constant, actively attending to and imitating same-gender models. Critics note gender-typed behaviour appears before constancy.

questions.stem: Why is Bem's gender schema theory able to explain gender-typed behaviour in children as young as two or three, when Kohlberg's theory has difficulty?
options: Schemas are inherited at birth and need no experience of the world
Schemas explain behaviour only in adults and older adolescents
Schemas begin forming once a child can label gender, before constancy
Schemas form only after children understand that gender is permanent
questions.explanation: Gender schema theory says children start organising information into gender categories as soon as they can label themselves and others, at around two to three years. Kohlberg's theory links active gender learning to constancy, which comes later.

questions.stem: A child is told a story about a female doctor, but when retelling it later says the doctor was a man. Gender schema theory explains this as:
options: the child reaching the stage of gender constancy in that story
a sex difference in verbal ability caused by brain organisation
information that conflicts with a schema being distorted to fit it
the child imitating a model of the same gender as themselves
questions.explanation: Gender schemas guide what children notice and remember. Information that does not fit the schema is often forgotten or changed to fit, as when a female doctor is recalled as male.

questions.stem: Fagot (1978) observed families with toddlers at home. What did she find?
options: Toddlers chose sex-typed toys only after reaching gender constancy
Fathers and mothers responded identically to all types of play
Parents responded more positively to sex-typed play than cross-sex play
Parents treated boys and girls in exactly the same way during play
questions.explanation: Fagot found parents encouraged play considered appropriate for the child's sex and discouraged cross-sex play, such as boys playing with dolls. This is evidence that socialisation by parents shapes gender behaviour from an early age.

questions.stem: Mead studied three societies in New Guinea. She reported that in one, both men and women were gentle and nurturing, and in another both were aggressive. What does this support?
options: Gender roles are identical in all societies
Gender roles are largely shaped by culture
Gender roles are fixed by biology alone
Gender identity depends on hormones alone
questions.explanation: Mead's reports that masculine and feminine roles differed greatly between societies support cultural relativism: gender roles are learned and shaped by culture. Her findings have since been criticised as overstated.

questions.stem: Which is a criticism made of Mead's research on gender roles?
options: Her observations may have been influenced by her expectations
She used a laboratory experiment that lacked any realism
She studied only chromosomes and so ignored the culture
Her sample was a large random sample of many countries
questions.explanation: Later researchers questioned whether Mead's descriptions reflected her own expectations and selective observation, a form of observer bias. Her work was observational fieldwork, not an experiment.

questions.stem: Evolutionary (sociobiological) theory explains gender differences as:
options: traits that improved reproductive success for each sex in the past
behaviours learned by watching and copying same-sex models
expectations that come from the jobs men and women now hold
mental categories that children use to sort information
questions.explanation: Evolutionary theory proposes that different reproductive pressures on males and females in the past favoured different behaviours, which were passed on genetically. Critics note it is hard to test and underplays culture.

questions.stem: Which finding would be hardest for evolutionary theory to explain?
options: Some sex differences appear very early in childhood
Gender roles have changed greatly within a few generations
Some sex differences appear across many different cultures
Males and females differ in average physical strength
questions.explanation: Rapid change in gender roles over a few generations is too fast to be explained by genetic evolution and points to social and cultural causes. The other findings are consistent with an evolutionary account.

questions.stem: The interactionist view of gender proposes that:
options: gender develops only once children understand that it is constant
biology and environment influence each other in shaping gender
gender is caused entirely by the social roles a society assigns
gender is determined entirely by chromosomes and prenatal hormones
questions.explanation: Interactionism holds that biology and environment combine and influence each other. For example, prenatal hormones may influence early preferences, which then shape how others respond to the child.

questions.stem: A study compares how often four-year-old boys and girls choose trucks or dolls. Why can a difference not be explained by biology alone?
options: Four-year-olds are too young to have any differences in hormones
Children of this age always choose toys at random without preference
Toy choice is a qualitative measure, so it cannot be compared
By age four, children have experienced years of gendered socialisation
questions.explanation: By age four, children have been exposed to parents, peers and media who model and reinforce gender-typed play. Biological and social influences are therefore confounded in such comparisons.

questions.stem: Much of the biological evidence on gender comes from case studies of people with intersex conditions. Which is a limitation of this evidence?
options: Intersex conditions are too common to be studied in any detail
Findings from small, unusual groups may not generalise to most people
Case studies cannot collect any qualitative data about gender identity
Case studies always use double-blind procedures, which lowers validity
questions.explanation: Case studies of rare conditions give rich detail but involve small, atypical samples, so their findings may not apply to the general population. Social influences on these individuals are also hard to control.
